extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, botanists, zoologists, and scientifically literate readers studying evolution and hybridism
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and evidentiary rules for judging explanations about natural selection, caste formation in social insects, and the sterility/fertility of first crosses and hybrids. Focuses on what kinds of observations, experiments, and comparative facts count for or against proposed mechanisms (inheritance, selection, domestication, systematic affinity, experimental artefacts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider family-level selection as well as individual selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection may be applied to the family, as well as to the individual, and may thus gain the desired end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin argues that traits correlated with sterility in some community members could be accumulated because fertile parents that produced more sterile offspring with the profitable modification would be favoured. Analogy: horticulturist destroys individuals but sows seeds from the same stock; breeder slaughtering animals still selects families that yield desired traits. Use family-level selection to explain correlated modifications among sterile castes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect and seek gradations linking castes as evidence of selection
rubrics_metrics.description: We ought occasionally to find neuter-insects of the same species, in the same nest, presenting gradations of structure; and this we do find.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin uses the presence of intermediate individuals (e.g., workers of intermediate size/ocelli condition in Formica flava, gradations in driver ants) as critical evidence that distinct castes could arise by accumulation of slight variations. Finding morphological intermediates between castes supports gradual selection-based origins rather than sudden special creation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use domestic-breeding analogies and experimental examples to test hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogy with domestic productions (horticulture, cattle-breeding) shows how desirable characters can be fixed by selecting parents rather than relying on individuals to reproduce themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: breeders selecting parents that produce oxen with long horns; horticulturists expecting nearly same variety from same stock even if individual plants are destroyed. These analogies are cited to justify plausibility that sterile worker castes could evolve by selection on parents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess functional advantage to the community as a selection pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: A slight modification of structure, or instinct, correlated with the sterile condition of certain members of the community, has been advantageous to the community: consequently the fertile males and females of the same community flourished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin treats the utility of division of labour (analogous to civilized man's division of labour) as a ground for natural selection acting at community/family level: traits that improve colony efficiency can be selected because they increase reproductive success of fertile members that produce those sterile helpers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain large differences by accumulation of numerous slight profitable variations
rubrics_metrics.description: Any amount of modification in structure can be effected by the accumulation of numerous, slight, and as we must call them accidental, variations, which are in any manner profitable, without exercise or habit having come into play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin repeatedly emphasizes gradual cumulative change: small, profitable, heritable variations accumulated by selection can produce prodigious differences (e.g., between fertile and sterile females). This is a criterion for plausibility of selection-based explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish sterility of first crosses from sterility of hybrids
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between the sterility of first crosses and of hybrids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin insists these are fundamentally different: first-cross sterility arises when two otherwise fertile parents produce few or no offspring together; hybrid sterility refers to the reproductive impotence of the hybrids themselves (organs may be structurally perfect but functionally impotent). Treat causes and evidence for each separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat fertility/sterility as a graduated continuum, not a binary
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of fertility, both of first crosses and of hybrids, graduates from zero to perfect fertility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin warns that sterility varies in degree and often 'graduates away'. Experimental counts show gradations; therefore one should avoid strict species/variety distinctions based solely on a binary fertility criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for experimental and cultivation conditions affecting fertility
rubrics_metrics.description: The fertility of pure species is easily affected by various circumstances (castration, seclusion, potting, being kept in chambers), which can impair fertility and bias hybridisation results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin criticises experiments (Gärtner) where plants were castrated/potted/secluded, noting these procedures often impair fertility. When interpreting hybridisation experiments, control for methodological artefacts (treatment, greenhouse/hothouse conditions, handling) that could reduce seed set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider effects of close interbreeding and outcrossing on hybrid fertility
rubrics_metrics.description: Close interbreeding lessens fertility, and an occasional cross with a distinct individual or variety increases fertility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin compiles facts showing inbreeding reduces fertility while occasional outcrossing restores it. He attributes observed progressive fertility decline in some hybrid lines to close interbreeding, not necessarily to intrinsic sterility of hybrids. Thus, experimental design must avoid enforced sibling mating across generations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise domestication can modify or remove sterility
rubrics_metrics.description: Sterility not a special endowment, but incidental on other differences; sterility may be removed by domestication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin suggests domestication can restore fertility between forms that were formerly sterile, e.g., many domestic animals now breed together though their wild progenitors may have been distinct. Do not assume sterility is irreversible or an innate 'mechanism' to preserve species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic affinity often correlates with crossability but with notable exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The fertility of first crosses and of hybrids is largely governed by their systematic affinity, though correspondence is not strict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generally species of the same genus/family cross more readily, but many exceptions exist (closely allied species that won't unite; distinct species that cross easily). Use systematic affinity as a guiding, not definitive, predictor of crossability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect reciprocal crosses to differ and test both directions
rubrics_metrics.description: There is often the widest possible difference in the facility of making reciprocal crosses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin gives examples (Mirabilis jalappa vs M. longiflora) where one directional cross succeeds and the reciprocal fails; hybrids from reciprocal crosses can differ in fertility. Always test both parental directions when assessing crossability and hybrid viability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish structural perfection of reproductive organs from functional fertility
rubrics_metrics.description: Hybrids have their reproductive organs functionally impotent, though the organs themselves are perfect in structure, as far as the microscope reveals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sterility can be functional rather than structural. Microscopic structural normality does not guarantee fertility; analyses must include functional assays (pollen viability, seed set) and not rely solely on morphological inspection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect individual and year-to-year variation in fertility outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of fertility is innately variable; it depends in part upon the constitution of the individuals chosen and on circumstances (even the same species crossed in different years may yield different results).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin cites Kölreuter, Gärtner, Herbert arriving at different conclusions; individual plants or hybrids from the same capsule may differ in fertility. Interpret single-experiment results cautiously and seek replication across individuals and seasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious using fertility as a sole criterion for species vs variety
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither sterility nor fertility affords any clear distinction between species and varieties; evidence from this source graduates away and is doubtful in the same degree as other constitutional differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin argues that since fertility/sterility is variable and affected by conditions, it should not be the sole decisive test for taxonomic rank; use a suite of morphological, reproductive, and historical/phylogenetic evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider natural pollination context (insect agency) when assessing hybrid fertility
rubrics_metrics.description: Horticulturists' hybrids often seed freely because insect agency allows cross-pollination among hybrid individuals, preventing the injurious influence of close interbreeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin notes that many nursery hybrids are fertile under natural insect-mediated crossing; artificial isolation or enforced selfing can underestimate fertility. Experiments should mimic natural pollination where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise some species/individuals hybridise more readily with other species than with themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: There are individual plants which can be far more easily fertilised by the pollen of another and distinct species, than by their own pollen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Hippeastrum, Lobelia, Passiflora, Verbascum where some individuals are sterile with self pollen but fertile with other species' pollen. Do not assume self-compatibility; investigate asymmetrical or surprising compatibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume any single recognizable morphological difference predicts crossability
rubrics_metrics.description: No one has been able to point out what kind, or what amount, of difference in any recognisable character is sufficient to prevent two species crossing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plants widely different in habit, floral structure, pollen, fruit, cotyledons, or ecology sometimes cross easily. Thus, reproductive compatibility may depend on subtle constitutional differences not apparent in gross morphology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat parallelism between difficulty of first cross and sterility of hybrids as imperfect
rubrics_metrics.description: Hybrids from species which are difficult to cross are generally very sterile, but the parallelism between difficulty of making a first cross and the sterility of the hybrids thus produced is by no means strict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are counterexamples (species that cross easily but produce sterile hybrids, and species hard to cross whose hybrids are fertile). Avoid inferring hybrid sterility solely from first-cross difficulty.
